questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The combination of academic opportunities along with possibilities for travel, exploration, and recreational activities.
It is a unique opportunity to live a routine-based life in a whole other country, and in doing so, be liable for economic support through scholarships, your home university, and welfare support (SU). I consider any well-timed opportunity for cultural, experiential, and existential enrichment a worthwhile endeavor; thus, there was no other option but to go on an exchange, given the fact that life is small, fragile, and unfortunately short. That is my reasoning for going on an exchange. It should be noted that I will also be spending time traveling the country after the academic exchange. 

Another vital matter to me is that after my graduation, I should have specialized not only in Sociology as a broad academic field of theoretical expertise, but also in certain aspects of sociology, and thus, the courses mattered a lot to me. By finding a partner university that offers subjects within my field og interest, I am focusing on a career path that overlaps with my personal inclinations.

These are the prospects of my motivation.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
1. Given the liberal state welfare system and capitalist incentives, students are very young. If you are older, you may be disappointed in your search for peers of a similar age. Despite this, the dorms are the best places to meet people, plan events, and join social activities spontaneously.
2. It's very expensive to rent dorms compared to other collectivised flats in the city. When I say cheaper, I mean 1,000-2,000 DKK more affordable per month. Wow...
3. The dorms are capitalist endeavors. You will pay 1500 DKK in entrée fee that you will never get back for 'administrative purposes' alone lol. You have to pay an extra 2,500 DKK if you want to cancel your contract before the time, even if you're months ahead in notice. You can't host guests, etc Be prepared with some extra thousand DKK.
4. Staff understands the bullshit system and will help you navigate it, they are super sweet :)) yay!

5. In the end, the opportunity to make friends across dorms in the exact location may outweigh the extra money you pay for the housing. I am an extrovert, so I found the opportunities here quite good. However, if you're more of an introvert, I (and other introverted people I met) recommend finding your own housing and joining uni events to make friends.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Haha, slightly. Well, I wanted to apply for psychological courses to specialize in that direction, but alas, KU Uni did not allow me to take late BA psychology courses, and Auckland did not allow me to take MA psychology courses, so I had to settle for a Pute Sociology degree. It was alright, haha.

However, I find it absolutely ridiculous on KU's part that you're not allowed to take BA courses towards your master's degree, and I see the argument that the difficulty and knowledge learned in these do not meet the standards and expectations of MA academia to be absurd. 
MA students are grown adults who choose to specialize in ways that are personally motivating to them. By not allowing cross-studies, regardless of level, we are collectively creating SILO thinking, demeaning students' ability to make meaningful and sound choices in their careers, as well as limiting cooperation and creative thinking between institutions. Bonkers?

We have sacrificed our trust in human creativity, resolve and potentials by putting our faith in standardized bureaucracy to dampen our fear of cynic behaviour that does not exist.

questions.answer: MA

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Master's degree programs. SO WELL ORGANIZED. Small units with space for questions and discussions. Emphasis on student discussions and group work, in contrast, I remember KU's courses as overcrowded, impersonal spaces with a strange top-down atmosphere.

The courses were made to encourage the production of potentially publishable work. It was composed of several assignments, each worth a different percentage of the grade. I found that it worked wonders in boosting my motivation, interest, and work ethic, as I built towards publishable material through the assignments, which I successfully completed. My confidence rose, and wow, yeah, the system works so well!

The difficulty was high, and so were the expectations, but they were catered to by interactive encouragement and solid feedback on all assignments. SO GOOD!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: In Western culture, there is practically no real cultural difference between DK and NZ other than the fact that it is located within a liberal welfare state, which makes people more inclined to partake in commercialized rituals—Merp merp. Very easy, there was no adjustment on my part :)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Practice your English beforehand. The easier time you have speaking and understanding English, the less of a barrier socializing and communicating will be. Be prepared to sacrifice some study time, actually, to experience some things! Life is short; at some point, you're going to kick the bucket. I'd rather have a surplus of lived experiences with people I like than dull memories of studies and work. :))

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing. I did not notice any specific cultural barriers or challenges.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Like any other colonized country, it is interesting to see immigrants and native white Pakeha ( foreigners) or 'kiwis' as they call themselves, navigate national identity and politics. Lol. NZ has done a decent job making Māori culture and history available throughout the country, so that is really interesting. They've done well from a post-colonist perspective, while still ofc. Maintaining colonist power inequities. It (Moari culture) is, however, very available for tourists, nice :)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
The most enriching part of this journey had been staying after my studies to travel the country. Just fucking awesome. In terms of exchange, then don't be shy about prioritizing having funnnnnn.
1. Momentum Mori, good grades are not worth your precious time. You have a unique opportunity to experience things you'd treasure forever! I made a distribution of 50/50. 50 percent uni, 50 percent travelling, and it worked wonders :))
2. Get a friend with a car or buy a car. NZ is accessible, but only by car, as there is far and wide between the epic spots! Join one or several clubs; they often organize transportation to distinctly awesome places! :))
3. GO TO FIJIIIIIII. I went to Fiji to renew my visa, as it is cheaper outside the country than inside ;) So if you want to travel, plan a trip outside the country, Fiji, Samoa, or Tonga in good time ;)
4. Ask locals or previous travellers for the good spots to go; a lot of insider info is available!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
APPLY FOR SCHOLARSHIPS! I planned this way, applied in good time, and spent hours writing applications. I almost forgot, but it is essential, and it paid off for me. (Danish scholarships are plenty) Good luck :)

Look forward to amazing lectores (At least in the sociological institute), wow! Aim to make something publishable. I find that the mindset at KU is to create to learn, but at UoA, it is creating to learn! So awesome.
Piercings are cheap in NZ ;))
Good coffee is also cheaper!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Being encouraged to and helped in producing publishable material. I feel like at KU, you're left totally to yourself without much interest or feedback from lecturers, or intimate classes in which participation is encouraged. I found the environment at UoA opposite!

Also, don't be shy to travel and explore :)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding similarly aged peers hahaa. But honestly it did not mean anything significantly. I had a smooth ride :)
